newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nose-cleansers take Japan by storm.
newsitem.headline: Nose-cleansers take Japan by storm.

text.p: Well-groomed Japanese women are awakening to the horror that a noticeable part of their bodies has managed to elude daily cleansing rituals, and the toiletry industry is profiting from the discovery.
"We envisaged the nose-pore cleanser market to be worth five billion yen ($45 million), but it has turned out to be more than double the initial estimate," Kao Corp. spokeswoman Minako Shimada said.
"Demand is so strong that our factories cannot produce enough to keep store shelves stocked."

This spring, after 20 years of intensive research, Japan's biggest toiletry manufacturer launched a peel-off facial treatment mask designed especially for the nose, igniting a nose-cleansing boom throughout the country.

Conventional masks were gooey substances that dried and hardened after being smeared onto the face. But the latest facials come in bandage-like strips that are wetted and then applied to the snout. The strips are yanked off when dry.

"Unlike regular peel-off masks, you can actually see the grime stuck onto the mask when you take it off so you feel really clean afterward," said Mayumi Ichikawa, a 25-year-old office employee. "It's remarkable how dirty one's nose can get."

Kao said the soaring sales of its nose-pore cleanser and other new products should raise its operating profits by about 3 percent in the current business year from 54.29 billion yen ($493 million) in fiscal 1995/1996 to March 31.
But analysts say the industry leaders are not the only ones profiting from the nose-cleansing fad.
Nippon Shikizai Inc., which recently listed its shares on the over-the-counter market, is also in the spotlight.
The firm does not market its own products but has some 80 client companies, including Kao and Amway Japan Ltd., for which it manufactures cosmetics or helps in research.
It produces a series of low-cost, algae-enriched nose and facial treatment masks in the old-fashioned rub-on form.

"The nose-pore mask Nippon Shikizai produces is selling especially briskly, in addition to the smudge-proof lipstick it invented recently and profits should rise because of it," said Akiko Koike, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre.
Industry watchers expect the firm's overall sales to jump 5 percent to 5.1 billion yen ($46.3 million), with operating profits rising 4 percent from last year to total 450 million ($4.1 million).
Daiwa Institute of Research analyst Shuji Hosoi said cosmetic trends, which are getting shorter and shorter, were providing wind for Nippon Shikizai's sails.

Firms need vast research facilities, manpower and production lines to keep up the stream of new products and they have no choice but to rely increasingly on outsourcing -- as in the case of the nose cleanser -- for items that may or may not sell, he said.

"The bulk of our business has traditionally been colour blending for various kinds of make-up," a Nippon Shikizai official said. "But orders for other products, like the now-trendy nose cleanser, are picking up."

Analysts say firms specialising in outsourcing take a 60 billion yen ($545 million) chunk of the 140 billion yen ($1.27 billion) cosmetic industry. Nippon Shikizai dominates with 10 percent of that share.

"Nippon Shikizai is an old and big name in the cosmetics industry and it may be one of the healthiest," Hosoi said. "If sales boom, their commissions rocket and if large firms go without a hit for a while, then orders for development and joint research to produce a million-seller come flooding in," Hosoi said. "Companies like Nippon Shikizai profit either way."
